implications.headline: Rising bad-debt write-offs, not the late-payment rate, are the real wedge
implications.body: The headline late-payment rate actually IMPROVED — overdue invoices fell to ~35% of B2B sales in 2025 (Atradius) from ~54% in 2024. But bad-debt write-offs rose to ~6% of B2B invoices (7% in agri-food). 'Customers pay slower' is a softening story; 'uncollectible losses are climbing' is the durable one. Anchor the pitch on permanent loss avoidance, not on slow payment.

implications.headline: The chasing cost — ~S$4,000/SME/yr — is the budget we redirect
implications.body: InvoiceInterchange puts the annual late-payment chasing burden at almost S$4,000 per SME, with ~52% of SMEs exposed. Most of that is internal time, not cash-out — so the sell is 'screen before you extend credit and avoid the chase entirely.' Pre-deal conduct intelligence is cheaper than post-deal recovery, which frames pricing against a known pain.

implications.headline: Incumbents score financials; nobody scores conduct
implications.body: Experian-DP, SCCB and Credit Bureau Asia cover financial-statement and litigation/winding-up data on most SG companies. None capture behavioural signals — bad-faith disputes, legal-threat bullying, undelivery, phoenixing across UEN+director identity. That white space is the defensible primitive, but it is also a cold-start data problem: value is near-zero until peer contributions reach density.

implications.headline: SOM is gated by trust-and-chill, not by addressable demand
implications.body: SAM (~S$80M) is large relative to a S$3.6M 3-year SOM because the binding constraint is not willingness-to-pay — it is the cold-start network effect plus a real defamation/POHA chill on honest negative feedback. Singapore has no anti-SLAPP shield, so contributors fear suits. Reaching even 5% of SAM requires solving contribution incentives and legal safe-harbour design first.

implications.headline: Construction is the beachhead vertical
implications.body: Construction runs the highest trade-credit dependence (~55% of B2B sales on deferred terms) and already has a statutory payment-dispute culture via the Security of Payment Act and adjudication. It is the segment most primed to value a counterparty-conduct layer, and SOPA adjudication records are a public, structured behavioural signal to seed the database.

market_size.methodology_appendix: Sizing is bottom-up and deliberately conservative; treat all figures as order-of-magnitude, not survey-census precision. The denominator is ACRA's business registry: ~614,000 active entities as of July 2025, of which ~456,000 are companies, against a widely-cited SME population of >300,000 (99% of SG enterprises are SMEs per SingStat/DOS, defined as <S$100M turnover or <200 staff). TAM is the sum of four adjacent spend pools the product competes for. (1) Commercial credit-report and risk-monitoring spend: we apply a ~S$400/yr blended figure across ~300,000 credit-extending SMEs (S$120M). This is an estimate — per-search bureau pricing (SCCB, Experian-DP, Credit Bureau Asia) ranges widely and many SMEs spend nothing, while heavier users spend thousands; S$400 is a population-weighted midpoint, not an observed average. (2) Debt-collection / chasing spend: InvoiceInterchange (2025) reports ~S$4,000/yr per SME chasing late payers and ~52% of SMEs affected. Most of that S$4,000 is internal labour, not cash-out, so we model only the externalised/outsourced portion (~S$400 across ~150,000 exposed SMEs = S$60M) to avoid double-counting time the firm already pays for. (3) Trade-credit-insurance premiums: APAC TCI was ~US$3.2B in 2021 (Allied Market Research) growing ~11% CAGR; Singapore is a mature node (Allianz Trade, Coface, Atradius all active; Enterprise Singapore formerly co-funded premiums via TCIS). We attribute ~S$50M of SG premium, consistent with the ~0.25%-of-insured-receivables rule of thumb. (4) KYB/onboarding/due-diligence: ~60,000 regulated and B2B firms running formal vendor verification at ~S$500/yr (ACRA BizFile+ pulls plus KYB SaaS) = S$30M. TAM ≈ S$260M. SAM filters TAM to firms whose pain is counterparty CONDUCT, not just financial scores, and who actually extend credit or onboard vendors: ~120,000 SMEs (derived from the ~54% of B2B sales transacted on credit per Atradius PPB Singapore 2025) at a ~S$650 blended annual willingness-to-pay = ~S$78M, rounded to S$80M. SOM is a 3-year obtainable run-rate for a concept-stage entrant facing a cold-start: ~6,000 paying SMEs (~5% of SAM) at ~S$540 blended ARPU plus ~S$0.4M pay-as-you-go token-lookup overage ≈ S$3.6M. The 5% ceiling reflects two hard constraints absent from a pure demand model: the network-effect cold-start (the database has near-zero value until peer contributions reach density) and a documented chilling effect — Singapore's POHA falsehood/disabling-order regime plus the absence of any anti-SLAPP statute means contributors of honest negative feedback face real takedown and defamation-suit risk. Key honesty caveats: the Atradius figures are panel-survey data (a sample of firms self-reporting), NOT a census, so the 35%/6%/46-day/54% numbers carry sampling error; the S$4,000 and 52% figures come from a single lender's (InvoiceInterchange) commentary and should be read as indicative; and the per-firm spend multipliers in TAM are modelled midpoints, not measured. Where a 2024-to-2025 comparison is made, note the direction is counter-intuitive: late payment improved while bad debt worsened, and the product thesis rests on the latter.

policies.title: Protection from Harassment Act 2014 (POHA) — falsehood, disabling & correction orders
policies.body: Since the 1 April 2020 amendments, POHA empowers courts to issue stop-publication, correction, targeted-correction and disabling orders against online false statements of fact, with standing extended to companies and other entities (not just individuals). A reviewed business that claims a posted statement is false can apply for a disabling order compelling an intermediary to take the content down — and these applications are heard swiftly. This is the single largest takedown and litigation risk for a peer-review platform.
policies.implication_for_us: Design for it: require evidence-backed, fact-anchored entries (invoices, judgments, SOPA adjudications), separate verifiable fact from opinion, build a fast notice-and-action takedown flow, and keep contributor audit trails. Treat a disabling order as a when-not-if and pre-build the compliance workflow.

policies.title: No anti-SLAPP statute in Singapore + defamation exposure
policies.body: Singapore has no anti-SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) shield, and defamation — both civil and the criminal offence under the Penal Code — remains a live threat for negative commentary about identifiable businesses or directors. A well-resourced counterparty can use the credible threat of a suit to chill honest reporting, the exact 'legal-threat bullying' behaviour the platform aims to surface.
policies.implication_for_us: Contributor protection is a product feature, not a legal afterthought: pseudonymous-but-verified contribution, platform-indemnification policy where claims are evidence-backed, structured rubric fields that resist 'sting' interpretation, and a moderation layer that strips unverifiable allegations before publication.

policies.title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (PDPA)
policies.body: PDPA governs collection, use and disclosure of personal data. Directors named by UEN+ACRA linkage are individuals, so their personal data falls in scope even where the conduct is commercial. Notification, purpose-limitation, accuracy and the right of access/correction all apply, and PDPC has shown willingness to act on reputational-data mishandling.
policies.implication_for_us: Lean on the legitimate-interests and publicly-available-data bases where applicable, but build accuracy and access/correction tooling from day one. Company-level conduct is lower-risk than director-level personal attribution — gate director-name display behind a higher evidence bar.

policies.title: Building & Construction Industry Security of Payment Act 2004 (SOPA)
policies.body: SOPA gives construction-chain parties a statutory right to progress payments and a fast, low-cost adjudication mechanism (Singapore Mediation Centre as the Authorised Nominating Body). 2019 enhancements extended payment-response periods and set a minimum late-payment interest floor. It establishes a public, structured record of who fails to pay on time in the sector with the heaviest trade-credit dependence.
policies.implication_for_us: Adjudication determinations are objective, hard-to-dispute conduct signals — ideal seed data for the construction beachhead and far more defamation-proof than user opinion. Ingest published adjudication outcomes to bootstrap the database before peer contributions reach density.

policies.title: Companies Act s.155A — director disqualification on 3 strike-offs in 5 years
policies.body: A director with at least three companies struck off by the Registrar (ACRA-initiated, not voluntary) within five years can be automatically disqualified for five years from the third strike-off, barred from any directorship or company management. This is the statutory fingerprint of phoenixing — serial abandonment of non-compliant shells.
policies.implication_for_us: Disqualification and force-strike-off records keyed to a director are objective, public, factual flags — the cleanest possible phoenixing signal and immune to the defamation problem. Cross-reference UEN+director identity against ACRA disqualification and gazetted strike-off data.

policies.title: Companies Act — phoenix / fraudulent & insolvent trading provisions
policies.body: Provisions against fraudulent trading, insolvent trading and reuse of an insolvent company's name target 'phoenix' behaviour where directors abandon a debt-laden entity and re-incorporate. Enforcement is case-by-case and reactive rather than preventive, leaving counterparties exposed at the point of dealing.
policies.implication_for_us: The law penalises phoenixing after the fact; the platform's value is preventive — warning a counterparty at the deal stage that a director matches a known phoenix pattern. Position the product as the early-warning layer the statute lacks.

policies.title: Insolvency, Restructuring & Dissolution Act 2018 (IRDA) — Simplified Insolvency Programme 2.0
policies.body: IRDA consolidates corporate and personal insolvency. The revamped Simplified Insolvency Programme (SIP 2.0) became a permanent IRDA feature from 29 January 2026, giving micro and small companies a faster, cheaper wind-down or restructuring path. More structured exits mean more recorded distress events tied to UENs and directors.
policies.implication_for_us: SIP/IRDA filings, judicial-management and winding-up records are public distress signals to ingest. A permanent, easier insolvency route may raise the baseline rate of recorded exits — increasing both the data supply and the underlying counterparty risk the product addresses.

cultural_signals.observation: Relationship-first, 'give face' (gei mianzi) trade culture makes SME owners reluctant to publicly blacklist a counterparty they may meet again
cultural_signals.evidence: Singapore's SME ecosystem is dense, locally-owned (~80%) and clan/association-networked; public negative attribution risks the relationship and invites retaliation, so owners privately warn each other instead of posting on the record.
cultural_signals.implication_for_us: Default to private, verified, pseudonymous contribution with aggregate scoring rather than named public call-outs. The product must let users contribute without 'losing face' — surface patterns, not personal accusations.

cultural_signals.observation: The informal grapevine already exists in WhatsApp and trade-association chat groups
cultural_signals.evidence: Industry WhatsApp groups, supplier chats and association mailing lists routinely pass around warnings about slow-payers and bad-faith counterparties — an unstructured, unsearchable, unverifiable reputation layer that already has product-market fit in behaviour.
cultural_signals.implication_for_us: Demand is proven; the wedge is structuring and verifying what already happens informally. Position as 'the grapevine, made searchable and evidence-backed' rather than introducing a new behaviour — far lower adoption friction.

cultural_signals.observation: Kiasu (fear-of-losing) credit-control instinct coexists with conflict avoidance
cultural_signals.evidence: SG SMEs are highly risk-averse on cash flow (kiasu about getting burned) — 60%+ intensified collection efforts per Atradius 2025 — yet culturally avoid open confrontation, creating a gap between wanting protection and being willing to speak up.
cultural_signals.implication_for_us: Frame the product as defensive self-protection ('check before you extend credit') not as an offensive blacklist. The kiasu instinct is the buying trigger; conflict-avoidance is why a structured intermediary is preferred over direct call-outs.

cultural_signals.observation: Defamation-suit fear actively chills honest negative feedback
cultural_signals.evidence: With no anti-SLAPP shield and a live POHA disabling-order regime, SG businesses know that an aggrieved counterparty can sue or force takedown; the 'legal-threat bullying' the platform documents is itself a reason users hesitate to contribute.
cultural_signals.implication_for_us: Trust and legal-safety design IS the growth lever. Visible contributor protection, evidence requirements and platform-side legal handling are prerequisites to liquidity, not nice-to-haves.

cultural_signals.observation: High baseline trust in government data and UEN identity
cultural_signals.evidence: Singaporeans transact heavily off ACRA BizFile+, SingPass and Corppass; the UEN is a universally accepted, trusted business identifier and the corporate register is among Asia's most transparent.
cultural_signals.implication_for_us: Key identity to UEN + verified ACRA director records to inherit that trust and prevent impersonation/duplicate-entity gaming. Government-grade identity anchoring is a credibility shortcut competitors of informal channels lack.

economic_signals.value: ~35% of B2B sales on credit (2025), improved from ~54% (2024)
economic_signals.implication_for_us: Late-payment frequency is falling, so the pitch cannot rest on 'everyone pays late.' The durable hook is the tail risk — the minority of counterparties that never pay — not the average delay.

economic_signals.value: ~6% of B2B invoices (2025), up from 2024; ~7% in agri-food, ~5% in energy/fuel
economic_signals.implication_for_us: Rising permanent losses are the strongest demand signal — write-offs are non-recoverable, so pre-deal conduct screening that avoids even one bad counterparty pays for years of subscription.

economic_signals.value: ~46 days from invoicing (2025); ~44 days in construction
economic_signals.implication_for_us: Roughly six-week terms mean a ~6-week exposure window per credit sale during which counterparty conduct matters — the natural moment to surface a pre-deal risk check.

economic_signals.indicator: Share of B2B sales transacted on credit
economic_signals.value: ~54% of B2B sales on credit (2025); ~55% in construction
economic_signals.implication_for_us: Over half of B2B volume carries counterparty credit risk — this is the SAM denominator. Construction's higher dependence confirms it as the beachhead vertical.

economic_signals.indicator: Annual cost of chasing late payers per SME
economic_signals.value: ~S$4,000/yr; ~52% of SMEs exposed to overdue-payment impact
economic_signals.implication_for_us: A quantified, single-source pain figure to anchor pricing against. Even modest deflection of this chasing burden justifies a several-hundred-dollar annual subscription.

economic_signals.value: 307 companies compulsorily wound up in 2024 (+52.7% YoY)
economic_signals.implication_for_us: A sharp rise in formal corporate failures means more counterparties going insolvent mid-relationship — rising supply of distress events to ingest and rising urgency for early-warning screening.

economic_signals.value: >614,000 active entities; ~456,000 companies (Jul 2025); >300,000 SMEs (99% of enterprises)
economic_signals.implication_for_us: The total addressable counterparty universe and the SME buyer base. Wide enough that even single-digit-percent penetration is a viable business.

adoption_patterns.note: Penetration estimates are entrant-model projections, not measured shares. SME uptake is structurally throttled by the cold-start network effect and the POHA/defamation chill on contribution; MNCs and larger firms already buy adjacent risk-intel (Experian-DP, SCCB, Dun & Bradstreet, Coface) and would adopt a conduct layer faster as a supplement to existing financial scoring, hence the higher figure. Both are 3-year horizon estimates.

trends.title: Open-government UEN & corporate data is increasingly machine-accessible
trends.evidence: ACRA BizFile+, data.gov.sg and the UEN registry expose entity, director and (force-)strike-off data; ACRA's register is rated among Asia's most transparent and digitally accessible.
trends.implication_for_us: Public structured data — disqualifications, gazetted strike-offs, winding-up, SOPA adjudications — can bootstrap the database with objective, defamation-proof signals before peer contributions reach density.

trends.title: AI and alternative-data credit scoring is moving past financial statements
trends.evidence: KYB platforms (Know Your Customer, Sumsub, QCC) and bureaus increasingly blend behavioural and alternative data; the market has 'moved beyond basic entity lookups' to ownership-mapping and screening workflows.
trends.implication_for_us: Counterparty CONDUCT data is the next alt-data frontier and the one incumbents have not captured. Frame the product as the behavioural layer that AI risk models currently lack an input for.

trends.title: Rising insolvencies post rate-hikes increase counterparty risk salience
trends.evidence: Compulsory windings-up jumped ~53% to 307 in 2024; bankruptcy filings rose ~25% in H1 2024; SIP 2.0 made simplified insolvency a permanent feature from Jan 2026.
trends.implication_for_us: A worsening distress cycle raises both the data supply (more recorded failures) and the felt need for pre-deal screening — a tailwind for adoption and a reason to seed insolvency data now.

trends.title: ESG and supply-chain due-diligence obligations are pushing conduct checks down to SMEs
trends.evidence: Larger buyers increasingly require vendors to evidence integrity and payment conduct as part of supply-chain and ESG due diligence; KYB is now triggered for loans, credit lines, BNPL and commercial insurance.
trends.implication_for_us: B2B conduct screening is shifting from optional to expected through procurement chains. A standardised peer-conduct score could become a vendor-onboarding checklist item, creating top-down demand.

trends.title: Embedded-finance and BNPL growth is multiplying KYB touchpoints
trends.evidence: Merchant onboarding, B2B BNPL and embedded lending in Singapore each require KYB at point of credit extension; KYB is now mandatory across loans, credit lines, BNPL, commercial insurance and investment services.
trends.implication_for_us: Distribution opportunity: embed conduct-risk lookups as an API into onboarding, invoice-financing and BNPL flows (e.g. InvoiceInterchange-type lenders) rather than relying solely on direct SME subscriptions.

trends.title: Trade-credit-insurance penetration is rising among SMEs across APAC
trends.evidence: APAC TCI revenue ~US$3.2B (2021) growing ~11% CAGR toward ~US$8.3B by 2030; SG insurers (Allianz Trade, Coface, Atradius) are actively pushing SME-tailored products despite premium-cost friction.
trends.implication_for_us: Insurers price on counterparty risk and want better conduct inputs — a potential data-partnership and distribution channel. A conduct score could feed underwriting or be co-sold with TCI to premium-sensitive SMEs.

trends.title: Regulators are tightening on phoenixing and serial non-compliance
trends.evidence: Section 155A auto-disqualification (3 ACRA strike-offs in 5 years), force-strike-off enforcement and IRDA reforms signal sustained pressure on directors who abandon debt-laden shells.
trends.implication_for_us: Regulatory direction validates the core thesis — phoenixing is recognised as a real harm. The platform complements enforcement by giving counterparties a preventive, deal-time signal the law only punishes after the fact.
